set1.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
set1.q: What does a hyperkinetic ventricular impulse indicate?
opts: Chronic pressure load with ventricular hypertrophy
That produces a SUSTAINED impulse, as in aortic stenosis or hypertension.
Chronic volume overload with ventricular dilation
That produces a DIFFUSE impulse, as in aortic or mitral regurgitation and cardiomyopathy.
Pericardial inflammation
Pericarditis produces a friction rub on auscultation rather than an altered impulse.
Transiently increased stroke volume
Correct, and it does not necessarily indicate heart disease — anxiety, hyperthyroidism and severe anemia are the examples.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 22

set1.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set1.q: What distinguishes tricuspid from mitral stenosis on auscultation?
opts: Its timing in systole
Both tricuspid and mitral stenosis are mid to late diastolic murmurs rather than systolic ones.
Its radiation to the axilla
Both have little or no radiation; axillary radiation belongs to mitral regurgitation.
Its location near the xiphoid

Correct — both are mid to late diastolic low-pitched rumbles of grade 1 to 4 heard with the bell, so location is what separates them. Tricuspid stenosis follows an opening snap. That is the lower left sternal border.
Its high pitch
Both tricuspid and mitral stenosis are low-pitched rumbles requiring the bell rather than the diaphragm.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 80

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
set1.q: What is a bruit?
opts: A high-pitched sound from a stenotic mitral valve opening

A high-pitched sound as a stenotic mitral valve opens is the opening snap, a very early diastolic sound of cardiac origin. A bruit is defined by the opposite origin: vascular, not cardiac. The tell: the opening snap is heard just medial to the apex, while bruits are listened for over the aorta and the renal, iliac and femoral arteries.
A murmur-like sound of vascular origin

Correct. A bruit is a murmur-like sound of vascular rather than cardiac origin, the distinction the stem's definition turns on. You listen for it over the aorta in the abdominal midline, the renal arteries 3 to 4 centimeters lateral to the aorta, the iliac arteries lateral to and below the umbilicus, and directly over the femoral arteries.
A palpable vibration from a loud murmur

A palpable vibration from a loud murmur is a thrill, felt with the balls of the hand pressed against the chest wall, not heard. A bruit is something you auscultate over an artery. The tell: a thrill is felt by touch over the heart, while a bruit is a sound over a vessel such as the aorta or a renal, iliac or femoral artery.
A scratchy sound from pericardial inflammation

A scratchy sound from pericardial inflammation is the pericardial friction rub of pericarditis, which is cardiac in origin and most often heard at Erb's point. A bruit comes from a blood vessel, not the sac around the heart. The tell: the rub is heard over the chest, while bruits are heard over the arteries of the abdomen and groin.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 106

set1.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills when using the stethoscope diaphragm and bell with relation to specific heart sounds
set1.q: Which sounds is the diaphragm better for?
opts: Bruits over peripheral arteries only
Bruits are auscultated in the peripheral vascular examination, but the diaphragm's cardiac role is the high-pitched sounds.
S1, S2 and rubs
Correct — the high-pitched sounds. It is pressed firmly and used to listen throughout the precordium. The regurgitant murmurs too.
S3, S4 and mitral stenosis
Those are low-pitched and are better heard with the bell applied lightly.
Only sounds at the apex
The diaphragm is used throughout the precordium rather than at one site.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 30

set1.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set1.q: What defines a pansystolic murmur?
opts: It begins after a click in mid systole
That is a late systolic murmur, following a mitral valve prolapse click.
It spans both systole and diastole
A sound heard through both is a continuous murmur or a pericardial friction rub.
It begins with S1 and continues to S2
Correct — something is open through all of systole, with blood flowing from a high pressure chamber to a lower one through a structure that should be closed. All are pathologic.
It occupies the middle of systole only
That is a midsystolic murmur, which may be innocent, physiologic or pathologic.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 72

set1.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
set1.q: How is dyspnea defined?
opts: An unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat

An unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat defines palpitations, described as skipping, racing, fluttering or pounding, not dyspnea. Dyspnea is about breathing, not the heartbeat. The tell: palpitations may come with anxiety or hyperthyroidism and prompt an electrocardiogram, while dyspnea is judged against the level of exertion.
Awareness of breathing out of proportion to exertion

Correct. Dyspnea is an uncomfortable awareness of breathing that is inappropriate to a given level of exertion; that qualifier, out of proportion to exertion, separates it from ordinary breathlessness after effort. It is common in both cardiac and pulmonary problems, and orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea are its positional and night-time patterns.
Breathlessness that occurs only when supine

Breathlessness that comes on when lying supine and improves on sitting up is orthopnea, a specific type of dyspnea quantified by the number of pillows used for sleep. Dyspnea itself is defined by exertion, not position. The tell: 'only when supine' names a trigger, while dyspnea is defined by a mismatch with the level of exertion.
Sudden breathlessness waking the patient from sleep

Sudden breathlessness that wakes the patient is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, usually about 1 to 2 hours after going to bed and prompting the patient to sit up, stand up or go to a window for air. It is one particular pattern, not the definition of dyspnea. The tell: it is tied to sleep, while dyspnea is defined against the level of exertion.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 7

set1.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set1.q: Which component of S2 is usually louder, and why?
opts: Aortic, reflecting the high pressure in the aorta
Correct. A2 and P2 are the two components, and the pressure difference between the two circuits is what makes the aortic one dominate.
Pulmonic, because the valve is closer to the chest wall
The aortic component is the louder one, and the reason given is aortic pressure rather than proximity.
They are always equal in intensity
The aortic component is usually the louder of the two, reflecting the high pressure in the aorta.
Whichever closes second
Loudness is attributed to the pressure in the aorta rather than to the order of closure.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 14

set1.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set1.q: What causes an opening snap?
opts: Rapid ventricular filling against a compliant ventricle

Rapid ventricular filling is S3 territory: S3 arises at the end of the rapid filling phase and is physiologic in children, young adults and late pregnancy. It is low-pitched, heard with the bell, with no stenotic valve involved. The tell: the opening snap is high-pitched, heard best with the diaphragm, and needs a stenotic mitral valve.
Abrupt deceleration as a stenotic mitral valve opens

Correct. An opening snap is a very early diastolic sound caused by abrupt deceleration as a STENOTIC mitral valve opens. It is high-pitched, heard best with the diaphragm just medial to the apex and along the lower left sternal border, and the obvious snap helps tell it from S2; as the leaflets calcify over time it becomes less audible.
Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves

Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves produces S2, a normal heart sound at the start of diastole. The opening snap follows S2 and can be mistaken for its pulmonic component when it radiates to the pulmonic area. The tell: S2 is valves closing, while the snap is a stenotic mitral valve opening, with a high pitch and an obvious snap.
Ballooning of the mitral valve into the left atrium

Ballooning of part of the mitral valve into the left atrium is mitral valve prolapse, which gives a mid to late SYSTOLIC click, often followed by a late systolic murmur. The opening snap is diastolic. The tell: prolapse is a redundant valve clicking in systole, while the snap is a stenotic valve opening early in diastole.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 44

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
set1.q: How long is the patient asked to clench the fist in the Allen test?
opts: Two seconds
Two seconds is the minimum thumb pressure for testing pitting edema.
Ten minutes
Ten minutes supine is the rest period before measuring brachial pressure for an ankle brachial index.
Until the patient reports pain
The duration given is thirty seconds of clenching rather than being guided by symptoms.
Thirty seconds
Correct, with both arteries occluded. The fist is then opened and one artery released to watch the hand fill.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 108

set1.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set1.q: What characterizes an innocent midsystolic murmur?
opts: A structural abnormality of the heart or great vessels
That describes a PATHOLOGIC murmur, such as aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Always grade 4 or above with a thrill
An innocent murmur is grade 1 to 3; a thrill implies grade 4 or above and suggests pathology.
No physiologic or structural abnormality

Correct, usually from increased blood flow. It diminishes when the patient stands, sits up, or performs a Valsalva, and is most common in infancy and childhood, though healthy adults can have one too. It grades 1 to 3 out of 6.
A physiologic change in body metabolism
That describes a PHYSIOLOGIC murmur, as in anemia, pregnancy, fever or hyperthyroidism.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 66

set1.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
set1.q: What does a sustained ventricular impulse indicate?
opts: Ventricular dilation from increased preload
That produces a diffuse impulse, from chronic volume overload.
Inflammation of the pericardial sac
That produces a pericardial friction rub rather than a change in the impulse.
Hypertrophy from chronic pressure load
Correct — increased afterload. Aortic stenosis and hypertension are the examples, and the duration is sustained rather than under two thirds of systole. That is increased afterload.
Transiently increased stroke volume
That produces a hyperkinetic impulse, which does not necessarily indicate heart disease.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 22

set1.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set1.q: What is the more common mechanism of S4?
opts: Turbulent flow across an incompetent valve

Turbulent flow across an incompetent valve is regurgitation, which produces a murmur, not a gallop. S4 comes from the atrium contracting into a stiff ventricle. The tell: regurgitation is a 'swoosh' of backward flow, while S4 is a dull, low-pitched sound just before S1 (Ten-nes-SEE).
Hypertrophy or fibrosis stiffening the ventricle

Correct. The stem asks for the MORE COMMON mechanism of S4: ventricular hypertrophy or fibrosis makes the ventricle stiff, so it resists filling after atrial contraction (decreased compliance). The causes follow from that, namely hypertensive heart disease, aortic stenosis, ischemic and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and delayed conduction between the atria and ventricles.
High filling pressures with abrupt deceleration of inflow

High left ventricular filling pressures with abrupt deceleration of inflow are the mechanism of a pathologic S3, the ventricular gallop, at the end of the rapid filling phase. S4 is the atrial gallop, tied to atrial contraction. The tell: S3 comes early in diastole after S2 (Ken-TUC-ky); S4 comes late, just before S1 (Ten-nes-SEE).
Sudden opening of a stenotic mitral valve

Abrupt deceleration as a stenotic mitral valve opens produces an opening snap, a high-pitched, very early diastolic sound. S4 is dull and low-pitched, late in diastole. The tell: the snap is heard with the diaphragm right after S2, while S4 needs the bell at the apex just before S1.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 42

set1.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
set1.q: What is the most common symptom of coronary artery disease?
opts: Chest pain
Correct, and the differential to hold alongside it is angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, dissecting aortic aneurysm and pulmonary embolism.
Palpitations
Palpitations are an unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat and do not necessarily indicate heart disease at all.
Syncope
Syncope is transient loss of consciousness with recovery, most commonly neurocardiogenic rather than the presenting symptom of coronary disease.
Peripheral edema
Edema is accumulation of excess fluid in the extravascular interstitial space, a later and more systemic finding.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 5

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
set1.q: What is true about the popliteal pulse?
opts: It is the easiest lower limb pulse to find

The popliteal pulse is the opposite of easy: it is harder to feel and may not be felt at all in some patients. You have to press deeply into the popliteal fossa to find it. The tell: an easy pulse would not need two named techniques, the knee flexed and relaxed or the patient prone with the knee flexed to 90 degrees.
Its absence always indicates arterial disease

An absent popliteal pulse is not automatically a problem: it may not be felt in some patients, and this may not be an issue if the more distal pulses are present. Check the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses first. The tell: 'always' contradicts the allowance for a patient in whom it simply cannot be felt.
It is palpated with the knee fully extended

Neither technique uses a straight knee: the popliteal pulse is felt with the knee flexed and relaxed, fingertips pressed deeply into the popliteal fossa, or with the patient prone and the knee flexed to 90 degrees, thumbs pressing deeply. The tell: 'fully extended' is the one detail that clashes with both methods, which share a bent knee.
It is harder to feel, and sometimes absent

Correct. The popliteal pulse is harder to feel and may or may not be felt in some patients, and this may not be an issue if the more distal pulses are present. To find it, flex the relaxed knee and press your fingertips deeply into the popliteal fossa, or have the patient lie prone with the knee flexed to 90 degrees and press with both thumbs.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 103

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
set1.q: What are varicosities?
opts: Mild to severe dilatation of veins

Correct. Varicosities are mild to severe dilatation of the veins, mainly in the lower extremities, which is the definition the stem asks for. They are one of the skin changes to look for, and venous varicosities are among the associated findings of chronic venous insufficiency, alongside edema, purpura, stasis dermatitis and cyanosis of the foot when dependent.
Thickened arterial walls with reduced elasticity

Varicosities are a disorder of veins, not arteries, so thickened arterial walls cannot define them. Arterial disease shows up on exam as absent or decreased pulses, which may suggest atherosclerosis or systemic embolism. The tell: varicosities are dilated veins you look for on inspection, while arterial disease is found by palpating the pulses.
Brown discoloration from hemosiderin

Brown discoloration from hemosiderin staining is a pigment change of chronic venous insufficiency, a consequence of venous disease rather than the dilated veins themselves. Varicosities are the veins, mildly to severely dilated. The tell: hemosiderin is a color in the skin, while a varicosity is a shape, a widened vein.
Ulceration around the medial malleolus

Ulceration over the medial and lateral malleolus is the typical ulcer of chronic venous insufficiency, with small, painful granulation tissue and irregular borders, not a varicosity. Varicosities are dilated veins. The tell: an ulcer is a break in the skin at the ankle, while a varicosity is a widened vein along the leg.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 95

set1.io: Review the classic areas of auscultation to assess cardiac sounds
set1.q: Which lighting is specified for the cardiovascular examination?
opts: Bright overhead lighting
Direct overhead light flattens the contours that inspection is trying to detect.
Dim lighting to reduce patient anxiety
Enough lighting and exposure is required; tangential lighting is the specific instruction.
Colored light to highlight cyanosis
No colored light is described; tangential lighting is what is specified.
Tangential lighting
Correct, because it casts shadows that reveal the contours of the chest wall — a pulsation visible in raking light can be invisible under direct light. It matters most during inspection.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 26

set1.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set1.q: How can palpating the carotid help with murmur timing?
opts: The carotid pulse identifies the murmur's intensity
Intensity is graded on the six-point Levine scale rather than by the carotid.
The carotid pulse indicates the shape of the murmur
Shape is the configuration of intensity over time, judged by listening.
Systolic murmurs match the carotid upstroke
Correct — a systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2, a diastolic one between S2 and S1, and the carotid gives you an external marker for which is which.
Diastolic murmurs coincide with the carotid upstroke
The carotid upstroke marks systole, so it is the systolic murmurs that coincide with it.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 50

set1.io: Define the physical examination findings of peripheral edema
set1.q: How is pitting edema tested for?
opts: Press on the nail bed and time the refill

Pressing on the fingernails and timing how long the nail beds take to turn pink is capillary refill, which checks the nail bed rather than testing for edema. The tell: capillary refill watches color return in the nail bed, while pitting edema looks for a depression left in swollen skin over the foot, the ankle and the shins.
Dorsiflex the foot at the ankle with the knee bent

Quickly dorsiflexing the foot with the knee bent is Homan's sign, which checks for deep vein thrombosis by looking for pain behind the knee. It tests for pain, not for fluid in the tissues. The tell: pitting edema needs pressure on the skin and a lasting dent, while Homan's sign needs a joint movement and a pain response.
Press firmly with the thumb, two seconds

Correct. Press firmly with the thumb for at least 2 seconds over the dorsum of the foot, behind the medial malleolus and over the shins; pitting is the depression the thumb leaves. Its depth and how long it lasts set the grade, from 1+ (2 millimeters, disappearing rapidly) to 4+ (8 millimeters, lasting more than 2 minutes).
Press with the balls of the hand against the limb

Pressing the balls of the hand against the chest wall is how you feel a thrill, the vibration of a loud murmur, not how you test for edema. Pitting edema needs the focused pressure of a thumb held for at least 2 seconds. The tell: the flat of the hand senses vibration over the heart, while the thumb leaves a pit in swollen skin.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 88

set1.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set1.q: Which states produce a physiologic midsystolic murmur?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and atrial septal defect
Both are pathologic structural causes of a midsystolic murmur.
Mitral and tricuspid regurgitation
Those produce pansystolic murmurs rather than midsystolic ones.
Anemia, pregnancy, fever, thyrotoxicosis
Correct — changes in body metabolism rather than a structural abnormality, which is what separates them from the pathologic group.
Aortic stenosis and pulmonic stenosis
Aortic and pulmonic stenosis are pathologic, arising from structural abnormality of the valve.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 66

set1.io: Review the classic areas of auscultation to assess cardiac sounds
set1.q: What is required of stethoscope placement?
opts: Placement over a thin layer of clothing is acceptable
The examination should never be done over the patient's clothing.
Contact anywhere on the chest wall is equivalent
The classic areas of auscultation are specific sites rather than interchangeable.
Firm pressure in every case
The diaphragm is pressed firmly but the bell is applied lightly.
Direct contact with the patient's skin
Correct, which is also why the examination should never be done over the patient's clothing and why the patient should be in a gown.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 30

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
set1.q: How should the patient be prepared before brachial pressure is measured for an ankle brachial index?
opts: Supine and resting for ten minutes
Correct, and the cuff is inflated 20 mm Hg above the last audible pulse then deflated at about 1 mm Hg per second, with two measurements averaged in each arm.
Seated with feet flat for five minutes
The patient is supine for ten minutes rather than seated, since posture alters the pressure.
Standing for two minutes
Standing would alter the pressures; the patient is supine and resting.
Immediately on arrival, with no rest
A ten minute supine rest is specified before the brachial pressure is taken.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 111

set1.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
set1.q: What does the Allen test evaluate?
opts: Patency of the radial and ulnar arteries

Correct. The Allen test evaluates the arterial supply of the hand by assessing the patency of the radial and ulnar arteries. Compress both, have the patient clench the fist for 30 seconds, open it, then release the ulnar artery and watch the hand fill; repeat, releasing the radial, to check that artery.
Presence of deep vein thrombosis

Deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a leg vein, checked by Homan's sign (pain behind the knee on forced dorsiflexion of the foot), not by a hand test. The Allen test looks at arteries, not veins. The tell: the Allen test is done at the wrist and hand, while deep vein thrombosis is sought with a maneuver at the ankle.
The ratio of ankle to brachial pressure

The ratio of ankle to brachial systolic pressure is the ankle brachial index, calculated separately for each leg with a blood pressure cuff. It assesses the legs, while the Allen test assesses the hand. The tell: the index is a number worked out from pressures, while the Allen test is a bedside look at how the hand refills.
The adequacy of capillary refill

Capillary refill is a separate check: press on the fingernails and time how long the nail beds take to turn pink. The Allen test compresses and releases named arteries at the wrist instead. The tell: capillary refill watches the nail bed as a whole, while the Allen test asks whether the radial and ulnar arteries are each patent.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 108

set1.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set1.q: How is an opening snap distinguished from the pulmonic component of S2?
opts: By its high pitch and obvious snapping quality
Correct, which matters because a loud snap can radiate to the apex and to the pulmonic area and be mistaken for P2.
By its low pitch and rumbling quality
Low pitch and rumbling describe the murmur of mitral stenosis that may follow, not the snap itself.
By its variation with the respiratory cycle
Respiratory variation is what characterizes physiologic splitting of S2.
By being heard only with the bell
The opening snap is heard best with the diaphragm, not the bell, because it is high pitched.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 44

set1.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
set1.q: What happens when a patient stands quickly from squatting?
opts: Blood pools in the legs; preload falls

Correct. Standing quickly from a squat lets blood move to the legs, so less returns to the heart (decreased venous return) and left ventricular preload falls. With less filling, the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur becomes louder and the aortic stenosis murmur gets softer, which is how this maneuver separates the two.
Blood returns from the legs and preload rises

Blood returning from the legs and preload rising describe the reverse move, squatting from standing or a leg raise, which forces stored blood back to the heart. Standing up does the opposite. The tell: on squatting the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur softens and the aortic stenosis murmur gets louder; on standing, the two swap.
Intrathoracic pressure rises

A rise in intrathoracic pressure is the Valsalva maneuver, forceful expiration against a closed airway as the supine patient bears down. Standing changes where the blood sits, not the pressure in the chest. The tell: both lower preload and make the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur louder, but only Valsalva strains against a closed airway.
Afterload rises through muscular contraction

Standing from a squat involves no sustained muscle squeeze; it acts on preload, as blood moves to the legs and venous return falls. A sustained squeeze is the isometric handgrip, which increases the murmurs of mitral regurgitation, mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation, among others. The tell: standing changes filling, not grip.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 62

set1.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set1.q: How is the murmur of mitral stenosis best heard?
opts: With the diaphragm at the base, sitting forward
That approach suits aortic regurgitation and the pericardial friction rub.
With the diaphragm at the apex, supine
The diaphragm at the apex is used for S1; a low-pitched rumble needs the bell.
With the bell in the aortic area
The aortic area carries aortic stenosis and the aortic ejection sound.
Bell at the apex, left lateral decubitus
Correct — a low-pitched decrescendo rumble, mid to late diastolic, grade 1 to 4, with little or no radiation.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 79

set1.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set1.q: Which conditions cause a pathologic S3?
opts: Pericarditis
That causes a friction rub heard intermittently through both systole and diastole.
Decreased contractility, heart failure, shunts
Correct, with the volume overload coming from aortic or mitral regurgitation — all conditions that raise left ventricular filling pressure. Ventricular volume overload as well.
Hypertensive heart disease and aortic stenosis
Those cause S4, through ventricular hypertrophy and reduced compliance.
Mitral valve prolapse
That causes a mid to late systolic click with a following murmur.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 40

set1.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
set1.q: What are the skin findings of chronic arterial insufficiency?
opts: Thin shiny skin, hair loss, cool to touch

Correct. Thin, shiny skin, loss of hair and skin that is cool to touch are the skin findings of chronic arterial insufficiency. The color is pale or dusky red, and the rest of the picture fits: no edema, decreased pulses, foot pallor on elevation, dusky rubor, painful ulceration unless neuropathy is present, and gangrene.
Thickened skin with brown pigmentation and pitting edema

Thickened skin, brown hemosiderin pigmentation and pitting edema are the findings of chronic VENOUS insufficiency, the other cause of chronic skin changes in the legs. Arterial insufficiency gives thin skin and no edema. The tell: thick, brown, swollen skin is venous; thin, shiny, hairless, cool skin is arterial.
Normal temperature with cyanosis when dependent

Normal temperature and cyanosis of the foot when dependent belong to chronic venous insufficiency, which also keeps normal pulses. Arterial insufficiency makes the skin cool to touch, and its color changes are pallor on elevation and dusky rubor. The tell: 'normal temperature' rules out the arterial picture, which is cool.
Warm erythematous skin with bounding pulses

Warm, red skin with bounding pulses is the opposite of arterial insufficiency, which makes the skin cool to touch and the pulses decreased. Bounding is the top of the pulse amplitude scale (4+), not a sign of reduced arterial supply. The tell: insufficiency means less arterial flow, so expect cool skin and weak pulses.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 91

set1.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set1.q: What can the murmur of aortic regurgitation be mistaken for?
opts: S3
S3 is a low-pitched early diastolic sound best heard with the bell.
Breath sounds
Correct, because it is high frequency and blowing. It is early diastolic, decrescendo, grade 1 to 3, from the aortic area down the left intercostal space.
A pericardial friction rub
A rub is scratchy and scraping, heard intermittently through both systole and diastole.
An opening snap
An opening snap is a discrete high-pitched sound rather than a sustained blowing murmur.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 77

set1.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set1.q: What produces a murmur?
opts: Closure of the atrioventricular valves

Closure of the mitral and tricuspid (atrioventricular) valves produces S1, the 'lub', a brief normal heart sound at the start of systole. A murmur is a longer sound of turbulent blood flow, not a valve closing. The tell: S1 is a discrete normal sound, while a murmur is a 'swoosh' heard across part of the cycle.
Inflammation of the pericardial sac

Inflammation of the pericardial sac is pericarditis, which produces a pericardial friction rub, a scratchy, scraping noise through both systole and diastole. A murmur needs turbulent blood flow, not inflamed pericardium. The tell: the rub is scratchy and comes from the sac around the heart, while a murmur is a 'swoosh' of blood over a valve.
Abrupt deceleration of a stenotic valve opening

Abrupt deceleration as a stenotic mitral valve opens produces an opening snap, a high-pitched, very early diastolic sound. It is a brief snap, not the sustained sound of turbulent flow. The tell: an opening snap is one sharp sound right after S2, while a murmur is a 'swoosh' that lasts through part of the cycle.
Turbulent blood flow over a valve

Correct. A murmur is the sound made by turbulent blood flow over a heart valve, and it sounds like a 'swoosh'. The turbulence has five named sources: flow across a partially obstructed valve, increased flow through a normal valve of a small child, ejection into a dilated chamber, regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve, and abnormal shunting into a lower pressure chamber.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

set1.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set1.q: In whom is S4 considered normal?
opts: Nobody — S4 is always pathologic
It is described as normal in trained athletes and in older age populations.
Trained athletes and older populations
Correct, which is the mirror of S3 — physiologic in the young and pathologic in the old, while S4 runs the other way.
Children and young adults
A physiologic S3 is what occurs in children and young adults up to about 35 or 40.
Women in the last trimester of pregnancy
The last trimester of pregnancy is a setting for a physiologic S3 rather than for a normal S4.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 42

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
set2.q: How is Homan's sign elicited, and what is a positive result?
opts: Quick ankle dorsiflexion, knee bent; pain behind it

Correct. The stem asks for both halves of the sign, and this option gives both: quickly and forcefully dorsiflex the foot at the ankle while keeping the knee bent, and a positive result is pain behind the knee during the maneuver. It is the test that checks for deep vein thrombosis, and a positive result has traditionally been thought of as a clinical sign of it.
Compression of both wrist arteries; delayed hand filling

Homan's sign is elicited at the ankle with the knee bent, so a wrist maneuver cannot be it. Compressing the radial and ulnar arteries, then releasing one and watching the hand fill, is the Allen test of arterial patency in the hand. The tell: Homan's sign looks for a clot in the leg veins, while this checks the arteries that supply the hand.
Thumb pressure for two seconds; a persisting depression

Thumb pressure answers a different question: whether swelling pits, not whether a movement hurts. Pressing firmly with the thumb for at least 2 seconds and seeing a lasting depression is the test for pitting edema. The tell: Homan's sign puts no pressure on the skin; it is a forced ankle movement with the knee bent.
Simultaneous radial and femoral palpation; a delay

Simultaneous radial and femoral palpation compares the timing of two arterial pulses and says nothing about a vein. A lag between them is pulse lag, which should make you consider coarctation of the aorta. The tell: Homan's sign is a maneuver on the foot with pain as its result, while pulse lag is a palpation finding with a delay as its result.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 114

set2.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set2.q: What usually causes a systolic click?
opts: Pericarditis
That produces a scratchy friction rub rather than a discrete click.
Mitral valve prolapse
Correct — abnormal systolic ballooning of part of the valve into the left atrium, from leaflet redundancy and elongation of the chordae tendineae.
Aortic valve stenosis
That produces a midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur, and may produce an early ejection sound.
Mitral stenosis
That produces an opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 39

set2.io: Review the classic areas of auscultation to assess cardiac sounds
set2.q: What should the examiner attend to about their hands?
opts: Long nails for precise palpation
Short nails are specified, alongside warm hands, a quiet room and adequate tangential lighting.
Warm hands and short nails
Correct, alongside a quiet room and adequate lighting — small things that determine whether the patient stays relaxed enough for the findings to be real.
Gloved hands at all times
Warm hands and short nails are what is specified for this examination.
Cold hands to provoke vasoconstriction
Warm hands are specified; cold hands would make the patient tense.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 26

set2.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set2.q: Which valves are open during ventricular systole?
opts: None of them
The semilunar valves must be open for blood to leave the ventricles.
The pulmonic and aortic valves
Correct — the right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary arteries and the left into the aorta, while the tricuspid and mitral valves are closed.
The tricuspid and mitral valves
Those close at the start of systole, which is what generates S1.
All four valves
The atrioventricular valves are closed while the semilunar valves are open.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 13

set2.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set2.q: Where does the murmur of pulmonic stenosis radiate?
opts: To the left axilla

Pulmonic stenosis does not radiate out to the left axilla; when loud, it spreads from the pulmonic area toward the left shoulder and neck. The other midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur here, aortic stenosis, goes to the carotids and down the left sternal border. The tell: the axilla is out to the side, while pulmonic stenosis travels upward.
To the right sternum and xiphoid

That pattern belongs to tricuspid regurgitation, which spreads to the right sternum, the xiphoid and the left midclavicular line but NOT the axilla. It is a pansystolic, blowing, plateau murmur at the lower left sternal border. The tell: pulmonic stenosis sits high at the pulmonic area and radiates up toward the left shoulder and neck.
Toward the left shoulder and neck, if loud

Correct. Pulmonic stenosis is a midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, medium-pitched harsh murmur heard at the pulmonic area, and when it is loud it radiates toward the left shoulder and neck. The 'if loud' qualifier matters: a loud pulmonic stenosis murmur also brings a thrill, and no maneuvers are listed for it.
To the carotids and down the left sternal border

That spread belongs to aortic stenosis, the other midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, harsh murmur, which often radiates to the carotids, down the left sternal border and even to the apex. The tell: aortic stenosis goes to the carotids from the aortic area, while pulmonic stenosis goes toward the left shoulder and neck, and only when loud.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 68

set2.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
set2.q: What should be remembered about palpitations?
opts: They are the most common symptom of coronary disease
Chest pain is the most common symptom of coronary artery disease.
They are only significant if they last over an hour
Duration is one of the things to ask about rather than a threshold for significance.
They do not necessarily mean heart disease
Correct — anxious and hyperthyroid patients may report them. The instruction attached is to get an electrocardiogram and to reword your questions if needed.
They always indicate an arrhythmia
Anxiety and hyperthyroidism produce them without any arrhythmia being present.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 6

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
set2.q: How is the ankle brachial index calculated?
opts: Brachial systolic over the higher ankle pressure
The ratio runs the other way, with the ankle pressure on top.
Lower of the two ankle pressures over the brachial systolic
The HIGHER of the two ankle artery pressures is used as the numerator rather than the lower.
Average of both ankle pressures over the average brachial
The higher single ankle pressure is used rather than an average.
Higher ankle pressure over brachial systolic
Correct, calculated for each leg and recorded to two decimal places. The normal range is 0.90 to 1.40.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 110

set2.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set2.q: What produces a pathologic S3?
opts: Turbulence across a narrowed mitral valve

Turbulent flow across a narrowed mitral valve is a murmur, the mid to late diastolic, low-pitched rumble of mitral stenosis, not an extra heart sound. A pathologic S3 comes from high filling pressures and abrupt deceleration of inflow. The tell: a rumble is sustained turbulence, while S3 is one brief sound right after S2 (Ken-TUC-ky).
High filling pressures, abruptly decelerating inflow

Correct. The stem asks about the pathologic S3, the one heard in adults over 40. High left ventricular filling pressures and abrupt deceleration of inflow across the mitral valve at the end of rapid filling produce it, like blood slapping against the ventricular wall; heart failure and volume overload from aortic or mitral regurgitation are among its causes.
Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle

Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle produces S4, the atrial gallop, from hypertrophy or fibrosis reducing compliance. S4 falls just before S1 (Ten-nes-SEE), late in diastole. The tell: S3 comes early in diastole right after S2 and belongs to the rapid filling phase, while S4 comes late and follows atrial contraction.
Sudden halting of a semilunar valve as it opens

Sudden halting of the aortic or pulmonic valve as it opens produces an early systolic ejection sound, a sharp, high-pitched click shortly after S1. S3 is a diastolic sound, not a systolic one. The tell: valves opening for ejection means early systole, while a pathologic S3 comes from filling in early diastole, after S2.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 40

set2.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set2.q: Which of these is a named cause of a murmur?
opts: Inflammation of the pericardium

Inflammation of the pericardial sac (pericarditis) produces a pericardial friction rub, a scratchy, scraping noise, not a murmur. A murmur needs turbulent blood flow over a heart valve or into a chamber. The tell: the rub is heard through both systole and diastole, while every named murmur cause involves blood flow.
Reduced ventricular compliance

Reduced ventricular compliance, from hypertrophy or fibrosis, produces S4, the atrial gallop, as the atrium contracts against a stiff ventricle. It is an extra heart sound rather than a murmur, so it is not one of the murmur causes. The tell: a gallop is a dull, low-pitched sound just before S1, while a murmur is a 'swoosh' of turbulent flow.
High left ventricular filling pressure

High left ventricular filling pressure, with abrupt deceleration of inflow, produces a pathologic S3, the ventricular gallop of adults over 40. It is an extra heart sound early in diastole, not a murmur. The tell: the named murmur causes are all about flow through a valve, into a chamber or through a shunt, not how the ventricle fills.
Ejection into a dilated chamber

Correct. Ejection into a dilated chamber is one of the five named causes of a murmur, the sound of turbulent blood flow that sounds like a 'swoosh'. The other four are flow across a partially obstructed valve, increased flow through a normal valve in a small child, regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve, and abnormal shunting into a lower pressure chamber.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

set2.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
set2.q: Which four diagnoses should always be considered with chest pain?
opts: Angina, infarction, dissection, embolism
Correct, and beyond them the task is distinguishing cardiovascular causes from pericardium, trachea, bronchi, parietal pleura, esophagus, chest wall, gallbladder, stomach and neck.
Pericarditis, pleurisy, esophagitis and gastritis
Those are among the non-cardiovascular sources to distinguish from, rather than the four to consider first.
Anxiety, hyperthyroidism, anemia and pregnancy
Those are the physiologic states that produce hyperkinetic impulses and flow murmurs rather than the chest pain differential.
Heart failure, valve disease, arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy
These are cardiac diagnoses but not the four named as always to consider when chest pain presents.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
set2.q: What happens to mitral valve prolapse on squatting or leg raise?
opts: It is moved later in systole
Correct, because the increased ventricular volume delays the point at which the redundant leaflet balloons into the atrium.
It becomes louder and earlier
Increased filling moves it LATER in systole rather than earlier.
It disappears entirely
The described effect is a shift in timing rather than abolition.
It becomes a diastolic murmur
The click and following murmur remain systolic; only their timing within systole shifts.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 62

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
set2.q: What are the findings of chronic venous insufficiency?
opts: Cool skin with decreased pulses and no edema

Cool skin, decreased pulses and no edema are the findings of chronic ARTERIAL insufficiency. Venous insufficiency is the reverse on all three: normal temperature, normal pulses and pitting edema. The tell: edema with normal pulses points to the veins, while cool skin with weak pulses and no swelling points to the arteries.
Foot pallor on elevation with dusky rubor

Foot pallor on elevation and dusky rubor are listed under chronic arterial insufficiency, with cool skin and decreased pulses. Venous insufficiency colors the skin differently: cyanotic or brownish hemosiderin staining and cyanosis of the foot when dependent. The tell: brown pigment means venous; pallor on elevation means arterial.
Mild or no pain, normal temperature, pitting edema

Correct. Chronic venous insufficiency brings a normal skin temperature and pitting edema, and the limb is listed with no pain; the only pain named is the small, painful granulation tissue inside a venous ulcer, which is why 'mild or no pain' fits. The rest of the picture: brownish hemosiderin staining, thickened skin, normal pulses, and gangrene that is rare.
Painful ulceration with thin shiny skin and hair loss

Painful ulceration with thin, shiny skin and hair loss describes chronic ARTERIAL insufficiency, where ulcers are painful unless neuropathy is present. Venous ulcers sit around the ankles, with thickened skin, hemosiderin staining and pitting edema. The tell: thin, shiny, hairless skin is arterial; thick, pigmented skin with edema is venous.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 93

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
set2.q: How is the carotid examined?
opts: Auscultate first, then palpate one side at a time
Correct, with the patient holding their breath, lateral to the trachea. Palpating both at once risks compromising cerebral flow.
Palpate both sides simultaneously to compare
The carotids are palpated ONE AT A TIME, unlike the radial and femoral pulses compared for lag.
Palpate first, then auscultate
Auscultation comes before palpation, so that the vessel is not disturbed before listening.
Auscultate while the patient breathes normally
The patient is asked to hold their breath, so breath sounds do not obscure a bruit.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 97

set2.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set2.q: How do diastolic murmurs compare with systolic ones?
opts: Always pathologic and always loud

Diastolic murmurs are not described as loud: they are more difficult to hear than systolic ones, and aortic regurgitation, for example, is only grade 1 to 3 and may be mistaken for breath sounds. The tell: 'always' appears twice, when the defining fact about diastolic murmurs is that they are less common and easy to miss.
Less common and more difficult to hear

Correct. Diastolic murmurs are both less common than systolic murmurs and more difficult to hear, which answers both halves of the comparison the stem asks for. That is why they need deliberate technique: aortic regurgitation, for example, is grade 1 to 3, high-pitched and heard best with the patient sitting, leaning forward and holding the breath after exhaling.
More common and easier to hear

This reverses both halves of the comparison: diastolic murmurs are less common than systolic murmurs and more difficult to hear, so the systolic group is the commoner, louder one. The tell: a soft, high-pitched diastolic murmur such as aortic regurgitation can be mistaken for breath sounds, the opposite of easy to hear.
Equally common but louder

Both halves are off: diastolic murmurs are less common than systolic murmurs, not equally common, and harder to hear rather than louder. Aortic regurgitation, a typical one, is a soft decrescendo murmur of grade 1 to 3. The tell: a louder murmur would not need the patient leaning forward with the breath held after exhaling to be heard.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 76

set2.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set2.q: How do aortic and pulmonic ejection sounds differ with respiration?
opts: Both increase with inspiration
The aortic ejection sound does not vary with respiration while the pulmonic one decreases on inspiration.
Both disappear with inspiration
Only the pulmonic sound decreases on inspiration; the aortic ejection sound is unchanged by respiration.
The aortic does not vary; the pulmonic decreases with inspiration
Correct, and their locations differ too — aortic at the base and apex, pulmonic best in the second and third intercostal spaces.
The aortic decreases with inspiration; the pulmonic does not vary
The relationship is the other way round: the pulmonic decreases with inspiration.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 38

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
set2.q: What should a radial to femoral pulse lag prompt you to consider?
opts: Chronic venous insufficiency

Chronic venous insufficiency leaves the pulses normal, so it cannot explain a delay between two arterial pulses. It shows instead with pitting edema, brownish hemosiderin staining and thickened skin. The tell: pulse lag compares the timing of the radial and femoral arterial pulses, while venous insufficiency is a problem of the veins.
Mitral valve prolapse

Mitral valve prolapse is found by auscultation, not by comparing pulses: it gives a mid to late systolic click, often followed by a late systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation. The tell: pulse lag is felt with two hands on two arteries at once, while prolapse is heard with the diaphragm at or medial to the apex.
Coarctation of the aorta

Correct. The stem's finding is a lag between the radial and femoral pulses, which you look for by palpating both at the same time. When that lag is present, the condition to consider is coarctation of the aorta. The femoral pulse used for this lies below the inguinal ligament, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.
Deep vein thrombosis

Deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a vein, so it does not change the timing of arterial pulses. It is the condition Homan's sign checks for, with pain behind the knee on forced dorsiflexion of the foot. The tell: a radial to femoral delay is an arterial timing problem that points to coarctation of the aorta, not a venous one.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 102

set2.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills when using the stethoscope diaphragm and bell with relation to specific heart sounds
set2.q: Which sounds is the bell better for?
opts: High-pitched sounds
The diaphragm is better for those — S1, S2, pericardial friction rubs, and the murmurs of aortic and mitral regurgitation.
Both equally
The two chest pieces are specifically suited to different pitches.
Only murmurs, not heart sounds
The bell picks up S3 and S4 as well as the low-pitched murmur of mitral stenosis.
Low-pitched sounds
Correct — S3, S4 and the murmur of mitral stenosis. It is applied lightly to the skin, ensuring no gaps, at the apex and moving medially along the lower sternal border.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 30

set2.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
set2.q: Where is the right ventricular impulse felt?
opts: Fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line

The 5th intercostal space at or just medial to the left midclavicular line is the normal spot for the point of maximal impulse, the LEFT ventricular apex, which marks the heart's left border. The tell: the midclavicular line means the left ventricle, while the right ventricular impulse is felt in the 3rd to 5th left intercostal spaces.
Second intercostal space at the right sternal border

The 2nd intercostal space at the right sternal border is the aortic auscultation area, where you listen to a valve, not where a ventricle is palpated. The right ventricular impulse is lower and on the left, in the 3rd to 5th left intercostal spaces. The tell: the right ventricle is felt to the LEFT of the sternum, not high on the right.
Over the carotid arteries

The carotid arteries are palpated in the neck for the pulse and to help time murmurs, not for a ventricular impulse. A systolic murmur coincides with the carotid upstroke, which is why you feel the carotid while listening. The tell: a ventricular impulse is felt on the chest wall, and the right one in the 3rd to 5th left intercostal spaces.
The 3rd to 5th left intercostal spaces

Correct. The right ventricular impulse is felt in the 3rd, 4th and 5th left intercostal spaces, and with pressure overload it may extend to the subxiphoid process. With volume overload, as in atrial septal defect, it lies along the left sternal border toward the left cardiac border; unlike the left ventricular impulse, its diameter is not useful.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 24

set2.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
set2.q: How is a patient asked to perform a Valsalva?
opts: Grip both hands tightly for thirty seconds

Gripping tightly is the isometric handgrip, a different maneuver that increases the murmurs of mitral regurgitation, pulmonic stenosis, ventricular septal defect, aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis. The tell: handgrip is a squeeze of the hands, while Valsalva is forceful expiration against a closed airway.
Lean forward and exhale completely

Sitting up, leaning forward, exhaling completely and holding the breath is the position for bringing out aortic regurgitation and the friction rub, not the Valsalva. Valsalva is done with the patient supine, bearing down. The tell: this position helps you hear sounds, while Valsalva is a strain that decreases left ventricular filling.
Bear down as if straining

Correct. Ask the supine patient to bear down as if straining during a bowel movement, or to push against your hand on the mid-abdomen. This forceful expiration against a closed airway raises intrathoracic pressure and decreases left ventricular filling, so a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur increases while an aortic stenosis murmur gets softer or does not change.
Squat quickly from standing

Squatting from standing does the opposite of Valsalva: it forces blood from the legs back to the heart and raises preload, so the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur softens and the aortic stenosis murmur grows louder. The tell: squatting is a change in posture that adds filling; Valsalva is a strain while supine that lowers it.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 61

set2.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
set2.q: Where is the brachial pulse found?
opts: At the lateral portion of the wrist

The lateral portion of the wrist is where the radial pulse is felt, not the brachial. The brachial pulse is higher up the arm, at the elbow, medial to the biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa. The tell: the wrist pulses are radial (lateral) and ulnar (medial), while the brachial pulse is the one at the elbow.
Behind the medial malleolus

Behind the medial malleolus is the posterior tibial pulse, a site at the ankle, while the brachial pulse is in the arm, medial to the biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa. The tell: a malleolus means the ankle, so this names a foot pulse; the other foot pulse is the dorsalis pedis, on the dorsum lateral to the extensor tendon of the great toe.
Medial to the biceps tendon at the elbow

Correct. The brachial pulse is felt medial to the biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa, which is the landmark the stem is asking for. Palpating on the medial side of the tendon, not lateral to it, is the detail that finds the artery. Farther down the same limb, the radial pulse is at the lateral portion of the wrist and the ulnar pulse at the medial portion.
Lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow

This has the right landmark on the wrong side: the brachial pulse lies MEDIAL to the biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa, not lateral to it. Lateral is the side that belongs to the radial pulse, but at the wrist rather than the elbow. The tell: brachial is medial at the elbow; radial is lateral at the wrist.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 98

set2.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set2.q: What produces the second heart sound?
opts: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves

Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves produces S1, at the start of systole, when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure. S2 comes at the start of diastole from the other pair of valves. The tell: the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) close for S1, the 'lub'; the aortic and pulmonic valves close for S2, the 'dub'.
Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle

Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle produces S4, the atrial gallop, an extra sound late in diastole just before S1. S2 is a normal heart sound made by valves closing, not by the atrium contracting. The tell: S4 needs reduced compliance from hypertrophy or fibrosis, while S2 is one of the two normal heart sounds, the 'dub'.
Turbulent flow across a narrowed valve

Turbulent flow across a narrowed valve produces a murmur, a 'swoosh' such as aortic stenosis, rather than a discrete heart sound. S2 is a brief sound made by two valves closing as the ventricles relax. The tell: a murmur lasts through part of systole or diastole, while S2 is the single 'dub' that marks the start of diastole.
Closure of the pulmonic and aortic valves

Correct. S2 comes at the start of diastole: as the ventricles start to relax, the pulmonic and aortic valves close, and that closure is the second heart sound. It has two parts, aortic (A2), usually louder because of the high pressure in the aorta, and pulmonic (P2), normally fused on expiration and audibly split on inspiration.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 14

set2.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
set2.q: When does paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea typically occur?
opts: Immediately on lying down
Breathlessness immediately on lying supine describes orthopnea rather than the paroxysmal nocturnal form.
In the early morning on waking
The episodes wake the patient from sleep rather than occurring on natural waking.
Only during exertion
Exertional breathlessness is ordinary dyspnea; this occurs at rest, during sleep.
One to two hours after going to bed
Correct — episodes of sudden dyspnea and orthopnea that wake the patient, prompting them to sit up, stand, or go to a window for air. Wheezing and coughing may accompany it.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 7

set2.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set2.q: What causes a pericardial friction rub?
opts: Reduced ventricular compliance

Reduced ventricular compliance, from hypertrophy or fibrosis, produces S4, a dull, low-pitched atrial gallop just before S1, heard with the bell. A friction rub is a pericardial sound, not a filling sound. The tell: the rub is high-pitched, best with the diaphragm, and scratchy through both systole and diastole.
Inflammation of the pericardial sac

Correct. A pericardial friction rub comes from inflammation of the pericardial sac, that is, pericarditis. It is a scratchy, scraping noise heard intermittently through both diastole and systole, high-pitched and best heard with the diaphragm, most often at Erb's point, and it may increase when the patient leans forward, exhales and holds the breath.
Turbulent flow across a stenotic valve

Turbulent flow across a stenotic valve produces a stenotic murmur, such as the low-pitched diastolic rumble of mitral or tricuspid stenosis, not a rub. The friction rub involves no valve; it comes from the inflamed pericardium. The tell: a stenotic murmur sits in one phase, while the rub scrapes through systole and diastole.
Regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve

Regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve produces a regurgitant murmur, such as mitral or tricuspid regurgitation, and is one of the named causes of a murmur. A rub has no valvular cause; it comes from an inflamed pericardial sac. The tell: a regurgitant murmur is a 'swoosh' of blood flow, while the rub is a scratchy, scraping noise.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 81

set2.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
set2.q: What is normal capillary refill time?
opts: Two to three seconds
Correct, tested by pressing on the fingernail and noting how long the nail bed takes to become pink again.
Under one second
The normal window is two to three seconds, so under one second would be unusually brisk.
Five to six seconds
That would be prolonged against the two to three second normal.
It varies too much to have a normal value
A normal of two to three seconds is specified, so the measure is not too variable to use.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 85

set2.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
set2.q: What is the cardiac cycle?
opts: The interval between S1 and S2

The interval between S1 and S2 is systole, the period of ventricular contraction, which is only one of the cycle's two phases. The cardiac cycle runs from the start of one heartbeat to the beginning of the next and includes diastole as well. The tell: S1 to S2 covers systole only; S2 back to S1 is diastole, and the cycle needs both.
From the start of one heartbeat to the next

Correct. The cardiac cycle is the period between the start of one heartbeat and the beginning of the next, made of alternating periods of contraction and relaxation. It is divided into two phases, systole (ventricular contraction) and diastole (ventricular relaxation and filling), so an option naming only one phase describes part of the cycle, not the whole.
The period of ventricular contraction only

The period of ventricular contraction is systole, one of the two phases of the cycle, not the cycle itself. In systole, ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure and closes the mitral and tricuspid valves, producing S1. The tell: the word 'only' leaves out diastole, and the cycle is defined by both phases alternating.
The period of ventricular relaxation only

The period of ventricular relaxation and filling is diastole, the other phase, so it too is only part of the cycle. The full cycle alternates contraction and relaxation from the start of one heartbeat to the next. The tell: this mirrors the systole option; whichever single phase is named, the cycle needs both systole and diastole.

set2.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
set2.q: What position brings out aortic regurgitation?
opts: Sitting forward, breath held after exhaling
Correct, and the same position is used for the pericardial friction rub — both are brought closer to the chest wall by it.
Left lateral decubitus with the bell
Left lateral decubitus with the bell is the position for mitral stenosis, S3 and S4.
Supine while bearing down
That is the Valsalva maneuver, used to distinguish hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Standing quickly from a squat
That reduces preload and is used to distinguish hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from aortic stenosis.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 77

set2.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
set2.q: What does a diffuse ventricular impulse indicate?
opts: Ventricular hypertrophy from increased afterload
That produces a sustained impulse, as in aortic stenosis or hypertension.
A transient rise in stroke volume
That produces a hyperkinetic impulse, seen in anxiety, hyperthyroidism and severe anemia.
Constriction of the pericardium
Pericardial disease is not the cause named for a diffuse impulse.
Dilation from chronic volume overload
Correct — increased preload, with aortic or mitral regurgitation and cardiomyopathy as the examples. The impulse is displaced left and possibly downward. That is increased preload.

set2.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
set2.q: Why is the murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy singled out as important to learn?
opts: Because it radiates to the carotids
Its murmur usually does not radiate to the neck, which is one of the features distinguishing it from aortic stenosis, where it often reaches the carotids.
So a sports physical is not signed off incorrectly
Correct — it is crescendo-decrescendo and midsystolic along the left sternal border, and missing it in a young athlete has obvious consequences.
Because it is the commonest murmur in adults
Aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation are far more common in adults.
Because it always produces a thrill
Its intensity is described as variable rather than always loud enough for a thrill.

set2.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
set2.q: Which questions help characterize edema?
opts: Do shoes or rings get tight? Eyelids puffy?

Correct. Edema questions focus on the location, timing and setting of the swelling and on associated symptoms, and tight shoes, tight rings and puffy eyelids in the morning ask exactly where and when the fluid collects. Asking whether it is worse in the morning or the evening, and suggesting a daily morning weight, round out the history.
How far can you walk before the pain stops you?

Walking distance before pain describes claudication, pain with walking that can progress to pain at rest in chronic arterial insufficiency, which has no edema. Edema questions ask about swelling: where, when and in what setting. The tell: this question is about pain with exercise, while edema questions are about tightness and puffiness.
How many pillows do you sleep on?

Pillow count quantifies orthopnea, dyspnea that comes on lying supine and improves on sitting up, not swelling. Edema is excess fluid in the extravascular interstitial space and is asked about by location, timing and setting. The tell: pillows measure breathing while lying flat; tight shoes and rings measure fluid in the tissues.
Does the sensation feel like skipping or fluttering?

'Skipping' and 'fluttering' are the words patients use for palpitations, an unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat, not for swelling. Palpitations do not necessarily mean heart disease and are followed up with an electrocardiogram. The tell: this asks how the heartbeat feels, while edema questions ask where the body swells and when.

set2.io: Review the point of maximal impulse and apical impulse
set2.q: Where is the point of maximal impulse normally found?
opts: Fifth space, at or just medial to midclavicular
Correct, and it identifies the LEFT BORDER of the heart — which is why a change in cardiac size or shape moves it.
Second intercostal space at the right sternal border
That is the aortic area of auscultation rather than the location of the apical impulse.
Fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border
The normal position is the fifth intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line.
Sixth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
That is where it may shift TO when the heart enlarges, rather than the normal position.
